meta.name: GM LS3 6.2L V8 -- rail connecting rod
meta.notes: The LS3 load environment with the conventional I-beam rod replaced by the rail rod concept: monolithic small end + twin steel rails, stabilising sleeve, big-end receiver, two swing clamps hooked into radiused rail notches, one tangential bolt. Every rail-rod dimension is a starting point, not a validated design.
meta.provenance: bore, stroke, rod length, bore spacing and compression ratio are published LS3 figures; all masses and the breathing calibration are estimates and must be replaced with measurements before any margin computed from them is trusted. Pin and rod section dimensions are reverse-engineered from published part weights and the journal size: they are self-consistent, not measured. All masses are now MEASURED from those solids rather than entered, so the design is internally consistent; the rod mass in particular disagrees with a commonly quoted figure and the geometry is believed over it

bore.why_min: subtractive manufacturing only: material comes off the block, never on, so the bore cannot go below the as-built 103.25 mm
bore.why_max: aftermarket piston availability: pistons are sold up to 103.50 mm (+0.25 mm over), so that overbore is established practice on this block

compression_ratio.why_max: knock limit on pump fuel; raise only with the fuel and boost level accounted for

bore_area.description: Piston crown area exposed to gas

clearance_volume.description: Volume above the piston at TDC

mean_piston_speed.description: Mean piston speed at the current operating point

speed.description: Engine speed at the operating point

crankcase_pressure.description: Pressure under the piston; opposes gas force

exhaust_pressure.description: Cylinder pressure during the exhaust stroke

fuel_lhv.description: Lower heating value of the fuel (gasoline ~44 MJ/kg)

combustion_efficiency.description: Fraction of fuel energy actually released

heat_loss_fraction.description: Share of released heat lost to the walls during the closed period. A lumped stand-in for a real heat transfer model -- see the limits section

ve_peak.description: Peak volumetric efficiency. Above 1.0 means the intake is tuned or boosted

ve_peak_speed.description: Engine speed at which volumetric efficiency peaks

ve_breadth.description: How sharply VE falls away from its peak. Small means a broad flat curve, large means a peaky one

ivc_angle.description: Intake valve closing; start of the closed period

evo_angle.description: Exhaust valve opening; end of the closed period

soc_angle.description: Start of combustion (start of heat release)

burn_duration.description: Crank angle for 0 to ~100% mass fraction burned

wiebe_a.description: Wiebe efficiency parameter; 6.908 gives 99.9% burned at the end of the stated duration

wiebe_m.description: Wiebe form factor; 2 is typical for SI engines

fmep_constant.description: Chen-Flynn constant term: accessory and valvetrain drag that does not scale with load or speed

fmep_load_coeff.description: Chen-Flynn load term, multiplying peak cylinder pressure. Covers ring and bearing friction rising with gas load

volumetric_efficiency.description: VE at the current speed, from the calibration curve

trapped_pressure.description: Cylinder pressure at IVC implied by the trapped mass

gamma.description: Ratio of specific heats used over the closed period. Below the cold-air 1.4 to account for hot burned gas

piston.description: Bare piston. Measured from the CadQuery solid, so the default state is self-consistent with its own geometry

pin.description: Gudgeon pin, measured from the solid

rod_total.description: Connecting rod complete with cap, bolts and bearings, measured from the solid plus rod.hardware_mass

rod_cg_from_small_end.description: Rod centre of mass from the small-end centre, measured from the solid rather than assumed. It lands at 0.700 of rod length here, which is where the usual rule of thumb puts it -- but only once the shank taper and the bolt bosses are modelled. Without them the solid says 0.62, and that error would land straight in reciprocating mass

rod_reciprocating.description: Rod mass acting at the small end

rod_rotating.description: Rod mass acting at the crankpin

as_built_bore.why: the block exists; the bore cannot be made smaller without resleeving
as_built_bore.description: Bore diameter as the block was manufactured

bore_spacing.why: 4.400 in bore spacing, fixed by the LS block casting

min_wall_to_coolant.why_min: below about 2.5 mm the wall distorts badly under head bolt clamping and cooling becomes unreliable

siamesed.description: True if adjacent bores share a wall with no coolant passage between them

liner_type.description: Thin iron liners cast into the aluminium block during casting -- the reason this block overbores so little

bore_profile.description: Bore cross-section: 'circle', 'polygon-N' or 'oval-R'. Only a circle can be sealed by piston rings; the others exist so the comparison can be computed rather than asserted

resleeving_allowed.description: If true, the bore may exceed the subtractive envelope because a thicker sleeve will be pressed in

catalogue_max_bore.why: 4.075 in. Forged LS3/L92 pistons are catalogued at this bore by Wiseco, Mahle, Manley and JE, so +0.010 in. over the 4.065 in. stock bore is established practice rather than an inference. Nobody sells a larger one for this block.
catalogue_max_bore.description: Largest bore an aftermarket piston is sold for

min_liner_wall.why_min: below about 0.8 mm a cast-in iron liner will not stay round under thermal load and can collapse into the coolant jacket
min_liner_wall.description: Minimum liner wall thickness to leave after boring

liner_thickness.description: Wall thickness of a cast-in or pressed-in liner. Boring eats into this before it reaches the parent block material

min_siamesed_web.why_min: a siamesed web carries head clamping load with no coolant behind it; thinner than about 1.5 mm and it cracks between the bores

gallery_offset.description: Bore centre to the near wall of the main oil gallery or a drainback. Not published -- sonic testing or a sectioned block

min_wall_to_gallery.why_min: breaking into an oil gallery scraps the block
min_wall_to_gallery.description: Minimum material between bore and oil gallery

head_bolt_offset.description: Bore centre to the near edge of a head bolt boss

min_wall_to_head_bolt.why_min: the boss carries clamping load straight into the deck; too little material and the bore distorts under torque
min_wall_to_head_bolt.description: Minimum material between bore and head bolt boss

min_sleeve_to_sleeve.why_min: interlocking sleeves may touch: at that point the sleeves themselves are the structure between the bores and the parent metal between them is gone
min_sleeve_to_sleeve.description: Minimum gap between adjacent sleeve outside diameters when resleeved

min_wall_when_sleeved.why_min: a pressed-in ductile iron sleeve carries the load the parent wall used to, but the parent metal still has to hold the sleeve
min_wall_when_sleeved.description: Minimum parent-block wall to retain around a sleeve. Smaller than the unsleeved minimum, which is the point of sleeving

replacement_sleeve_wall.why_min: a pressed-in ductile iron sleeve thinner than about 2 mm distorts when it is pressed and will not hold round
replacement_sleeve_wall.description: Wall thickness of the sleeve used when resleeving

mass_ceiling_reciprocating.description: Optional ceiling on reciprocating mass per cylinder

min_safety_factor.description: Minimum acceptable safety factor on any component

wall_thickness_measured.description: Measured bore wall thickness at its thinnest point. Set this from a sonic test; until then the tool falls back to a bore-spacing estimate

wall_thickness.description: Bore wall thickness used for the hoop stress model

crown_thickness.why_min: below about 2.5 mm a crown cannot carry peak firing pressure or conduct its own heat away
crown_thickness.description: Crown thickness at its thinnest section

crown_support_radius_fraction.description: Largest unsupported crown radius, as a fraction of the bore radius. A real crown is braced underneath by the pin bosses and around its rim by the ring belt, so it spans far less than the full bore. THIS IS THE BIGGEST APPROXIMATION IN THE CROWN MODEL: the stress scales with its square, and the default was CALIBRATED so that a production piston sits just above its fatigue limit at redline, not derived from anything. Only FEA on real geometry settles it

thermal_constraint_factor.description: Fraction of free thermal expansion the crown is actually restrained from making. Drives the thermal-fatigue estimate almost single-handedly

skirt_length.why: capped at the skirt the geometry actually has: 44.0 mm total height less the 17.4 mm ring belt. Was 30.0 mm, which was longer than the panel it was supposed to be measuring
skirt_length.why_max: the skirt panel is only 26.60 mm long (44.0 mm total height less the 17.4 mm ring belt); the bearing length cannot exceed it

skirt_bearing_arc.description: Fraction of the full projected area that bears. The standard convention for skirt specific pressure uses the whole projected area, skirt length x bore, the same way journal bearing pressure is defined -- so 1.0 matches published allowables. Reduce it only if you also reduce the allowable to match

top_land_height.why_min: a shorter top land cracks under peak pressure and runs too hot
top_land_height.description: Axial height from the crown face to the top ring groove

ring_groove_depth.description: Radial depth of the top ring groove

ring_axial_height.description: Axial height of the top ring

boss_inner_span.description: Clear gap between the two pin bosses; the rod small end runs in it

allowable_skirt_pressure.description: Specific pressure at which the skirt starts to scuff, on the full-projected-area convention. Published practice spans roughly 1.5 to 3 MPa depending on skirt coating, oil and bore finish: a band, not a sharp limit

allowable_groove_pressure.description: Groove flank pressure an aluminium piston tolerates before the groove starts to pound out

compression_height.description: Crown face to pin centre. With rod length and crank radius this fixes where the crown sits at TDC

total_height.description: Crown face to the bottom of the skirt

wall_thickness.why_min: below about 1.2 mm the ring belt wall cannot be cast or machined reliably
wall_thickness.description: Radial wall from the ring groove root inward to the under-crown cavity

second_land_height.description: Height of the lands between the ring grooves

oil_ring_height.description: Axial height of the oil ring groove

oil_groove_depth.description: Radial depth of the oil ring groove

crown_dish_volume.description: Volume cut out of the crown face. Positive dishes the crown and lowers compression ratio; zero is flat

boss_width_factor.description: Width of the pin boss pad across the thrust axis, as a multiple of pin diameter. Wider spreads the boss bore pressure and costs reciprocating mass

skirt_width_fraction.description: Width of the skirt across the thrust faces, as a fraction of the bore. Material outside it is relieved at the pin-axis ends. Distinct from skirt_bearing_arc, which is a pressure convention

ring_belt_height.description: Crown face to the bottom of the oil ring groove

ring_groove_root_diameter.description: Diameter at the bottom of the groove

skirt_bearing_area.description: Projected area of one skirt face

inner_diameter.description: Pin bore. Bigger saves reciprocating mass and costs bending stiffness -- the classic piston trade

support_span_factor.description: Where the boss reaction acts, between the boss inner edge (0.0) and the boss centroid (1.0). Real boss pressure peaks near the inner edge but is not concentrated there, so the truth is in between. Like the crown support radius, this was calibrated so that a production pin passes, and only FEA settles it

max_ovality.description: Allowable increase in horizontal diameter under load. Beyond roughly 0.07 mm the boss bore fatigues

bending_span.description: Effective support span between the pin bosses

bushing_width.description: Axial width of the small-end bore

material.description: Bushing material, or the rod material for a bushingless small end

allowable_pressure.description: Projected specific pressure the bushing tolerates in compression

shank_height.description: Section height in the plane of rotation

shank_width.description: Flange width, measured along the crank axis

shank_web.why_min: a thinner web cannot be forged or machined reliably
shank_web.description: Web thickness of the I or H section

shank_taper.description: How much larger the shank section is at the big end than at the small end. The shank_* dimensions describe the MINIMUM section, which is what the tension and buckling checks use

k_in_plane.description: Effective-length factor for buckling in the plane of rotation. 1.0 = pinned at both ends, which is what the pin and crankpin actually provide

k_out_of_plane.description: Effective-length factor out of plane, where the pin bosses and big end restrain rotation

small_end_outer_diameter.description: Outside diameter of the small end

big_end_outer_diameter.description: Outside diameter of the big end

bearing_clearance.description: Radial running clearance of the big-end bearing

allowable_bearing_pressure.description: Projected specific pressure for a trimetal shell

hardware_mass.description: Rod bolts, bearing shells and cap features the solid model does not carry. Treated as lumped at the big end centre, which is where they sit

joint_stiffness_factor.description: Share of the external load the bolt takes. 0.2 to 0.3 for a stiff rod joint

surface_finish.description: Rolled threads behave better than this suggests; the benefit is not credited

cap_mass.description: Rod cap plus its bearing shell. Its centrifugal force adds to the bolt load at TDC

crown_heat_share.description: Share of wall heat rejection that goes into the piston rather than the head or the liner

conductance_rings.description: Piston to liner through the ring pack; the dominant path out of a piston

conductance_skirt.description: Piston to liner through the skirt

conductance_oil.description: Underside to oil. Raise this for a cooling jet or a gallery-cooled piston

reliability.description: Reliability the endurance limit is corrected for

design_life_cycles.description: Target life. 10^8 cycles is about 480 hours at 3500 rpm for a part loaded once per revolution

kf_crown.description: Fatigue notch factor at the crown-to-wall junction

kf_land.description: Notch factor at the ring groove root, a sharp corner

kf_pin.description: Notch factor for the pin; a plain tube, so mild

kf_rod.description: Notch factor at the shank-to-end transitions

kf_bolt.description: Notch factor at the thread root. Already implicit in the bolt fatigue method, so it is reported rather than applied twice

enabled.description: Use the rail connecting rod (monolithic small end + twin steel rails, stabilising sleeve, big-end receiver, two swing clamps, one tangential bolt) in place of the conventional I-beam rod

eye_outer_diameter.description: Outside diameter of the small-end eye. Its bore is the gudgeon pin diameter and its width is small_end.bushing_width

rail_outer_span.description: Distance between the OUTSIDE faces of the two rails. This is the strict envelope the sleeve slides over, so nothing below the eye may exceed it

rail_width.why_min: a rail thinner than about 2.5 mm has nothing left under its locking notch
rail_width.why_max: the two rails would meet on the rod axis
rail_width.description: Rail thickness in the plane of rotation (x). The notch is cut into this dimension

rail_depth.description: Rail depth along the crank axis (y). Out-of-plane buckling rests almost entirely on this

eye_transition_radius.description: Blend radius where the rails run into the eye

notch_depth.why_max: a notch deeper than 60% of the rail width leaves too little net section to carry tension
notch_depth.description: Depth of the locking notch at its deepest point, measured in from the rail's outside face

notch_ramp_angle.description: Angle of the tapered ramp from the rail axis. Steeper holds the rail with less lateral pry per newton of tension but makes a shorter, more abrupt recess

notch_top_radius.why_min: the top radius must be at least the 1.20 mm notch depth, or the recess needs a step or an undercut to return to the rail face -- the concept requires a radiused transition, not a stepped pocket or a hook
notch_top_radius.description: Radius of the deepest/top transition of the notch. It is also the clamp knob's socket, and the knob is the swing pivot. Bounded below by the notch depth: a smaller radius cannot reach back to the rail face without a step or an undercut, which the concept rules out

notch_lower_radius.description: Blend radius where the ramp returns to full rail width

rail_land_length.description: Length from the rail's flat bottom face up to where the ramp would meet the full-width face. The full-width land below the notch is this less the lower blend

receiver_arc_half_angle.description: Half the angle of crankpin bore the receiver wraps, measured from the rod axis. The swing clamps wrap the rest

receiver_floor_thickness.description: Thinnest material between the crankpin bore and the floor a rail seats on

receiver_tip_angle.description: Included angle at the receiver's lower corners, between the bore and the flank. Small is a knife edge; large pushes the clamp arm outward

edge_radius.description: Radius every convex corner of the receiver and the clamps is broken to

clamp_thickness.description: Radial thickness of each clamp around the crankpin

arm_thickness.description: Thickness of the clamp arm where it runs up the receiver flank to the rail

tip_clearance.description: Gap between the knob/flank and the rail notch they conform to. Geometric: the contact network treats the seated joint as closed

seat_interference.description: Designed overlap between the clamp's knob and flank and the rail notch in the nominal closed position. Positive means the tip has to be forced into the notch, so the bolt preload drives the rail foot down onto the receiver floor -- the only way the joint carries preload at the notch at all. Zero is line-to-line; negative is a running gap

guide_clearance.description: Gap between the clamp and the receiver flank and scoop in the closed position. The contact network closes it only if the joint deflects that far

lug_gap.description: Gap between the two lug faces at assembly, before preload. With a gap the bolt clamps the crankpin rather than the lugs

lug_length.description: Length of each lug along the bolt axis

lug_wall.description: Material below the bolt hole at the bottom of the lug

shell_mass.description: Big-end bearing shells, the one piece of rod hardware not modelled as a solid. Lumped at the crankpin centre

bigend_material.description: Material of the receiver and both clamps

bolt_offset.description: Distance from the crankpin bore surface to the bolt axis, straight down

bolt_preload.description: Assembly preload in the single tangential bolt

bolt_finish.description: Rolled threads are better than this credits

sleeve_material.description: The concept leaves this open. Candidates in the database: CFRP-quasi-iso, PEEK-CF30, AZ80-T5, 7075-T6, Ti-6Al-4V

sleeve_wall.description: Sleeve wall outside the rails, in x and in y

sleeve_clearance.description: Clearance between each rail and its sleeve channel

sleeve_end_gap.description: Gap between the sleeve and the eye at the top, and between the sleeve and the clamp tips at the bottom

bracing_fraction.description: Lateral force the sleeve must supply to keep the rails straight, as a fraction of rod compression. The classical bracing rule is 1-2%

contact_depth.description: Effective compliant depth behind each contact patch, setting contact stiffness as E * area / depth. The network treats the parts as rigid, so this is where all of their elasticity is lumped. Load SHARING between redundant contacts depends on it; statically determinate paths do not

rail_engagement.why_min: the notch has to finish below the floor of the sleeve seat, or the clamp is reaching over the top of the receiver instead of through its wall
rail_engagement.description: How deep each rail sits in the receiver, from its flat foot up to the floor of the sleeve seat. The locking notch lives inside this depth, so the swing clamp reaches it through the receiver's own wall rather than over the top

receiver_wall.description: Material outboard of each rail slot at the top of the receiver. This is the wall the curved swing channel is cut through, so it has to be thicker than the channel is deep

receiver_rim.description: Material left above the channel mouth, between it and the receiver's top face

slot_clearance.description: Clearance between a rail and the slot it drops into in the receiver

seat_depth.description: Depth of the inset seat machined into the receiver's top face. The bottom of the stabilising sleeve lands in it; the rails carry on down through its floor into their slots

seat_clearance.description: Clearance between the sleeve and the walls of the seat it sits in

swing_radius.description: Radius of the swing channel's centreline. This is the dimension that DEFINES the swing: the pivot is the centre of this arc, and it lies on no part -- it floats above the rail, outside every solid. A larger radius makes the clamp enter flatter and drive more squarely into the notch; a smaller one makes it drop in more steeply

swing_pivot_lean.description: Where the pivot sits, as an angle from straight up, leaning OUT away from the rod axis, seen from the seated clamp tip. It has to lean out: lean it in and the pivot lands inside the rail or the sleeve, and the layout refuses it, because a pivot on a part is a part acting as the hinge. Leaning it out also tips the tip's travel, so the clamp swings down onto the crankpin as it closes rather than sliding straight sideways into the notch

swing_open_angle.description: How far back the clamp swings from seated. The channel through the receiver is the clamp's tongue swept through this angle, so it is what makes the channel a channel rather than a slot

channel_thickness.description: Radial thickness of the swing channel, and so of the clamp tongue that runs in it. Its width along the crank axis is not a free parameter: it is the rail depth, because the tongue has to fill the notch front to back

channel_clearance.description: Clearance between the clamp tongue and the walls of the channel it swings in

sleeve_core.description: What fills the web between the two rail skins: 'sheet-gyroid' for the printed lattice, 'solid' for the original one-piece sleeve. Everything else about the sleeve is the same either way

sleeve_skin.why_min: a skin thinner than half a millimetre cannot be held flat through machining, let alone bear on a rail
sleeve_skin.description: Thickness of the solid skin wrapped round each rail channel, AFTER machining. These are the only surfaces on the sleeve that touch anything, and both channels are machined in one fixture so they stay parallel. Thicker skins eat the lattice core from both sides, and the core has to stay at least four cells wide for its effective properties to mean anything

sleeve_face_shell.description: Thickness of the thin solid shell on each of the sleeve's two big faces. Ties the two rail skins together and makes the part handleable; set it to zero to leave the lattice open on both faces, which is the easiest thing in the world to get powder out of and the least stiff

machining_allowance.description: Stock left on the printed rail channels for the single machining fixture. The skin is PRINTED at sleeve_skin plus this and machined back

lattice_cell.description: Gyroid unit cell. It fights itself from both ends: a smaller cell fits more cells across the core (which homogenisation needs) but thins the sheet below what the machine can print at a given density, and a larger cell does the reverse

lattice_density.description: Relative density of the lattice at the sleeve's MID-LENGTH, where the shear it carries is least. This is the number to sweep: the web's shear stiffness is what turns two rails into one column, so it lands straight on the buckling margins

lattice_end_density.description: Relative density at each END of the sleeve. Denser than mid-length on purpose: a shear web's demand is V = dM/dz, which peaks at the ends and vanishes at mid-length, the opposite of the bending moment

lattice_grading_exponent.description: How the density runs from mid-length to the ends, as |s|^exponent. 1 is linear; higher keeps the light middle for longer and puts the transition nearer the ends

lattice_min_wall.description: Thinnest sheet the machine will print. The binding station is wherever the graded density is LOWEST, not the average. Replace with your own machine's figure

lattice_ports.description: Powder ports through the face shells, on the cell pitch. With shells on both faces and a rail skin on each side the core is closed on four sides and drains only along its own length; the ports cut that path by an order of magnitude. Irrelevant if sleeve_face_shell is zero

lattice_port_diameter.description: Diameter of each powder port through the face shells

lattice_modulus_coefficient.description: C in E*/Es = C rho^n for the sheet gyroid. A CALIBRATED GUESS from published sheet-TPMS fits, not a measurement. Every lattice stiffness in this tool rests on it, so it is the first thing to replace with compression coupons off your own machine in your own build orientation

lattice_modulus_exponent.description: n in E*/Es = C rho^n. Near 1 is stretch-dominated, near 2 is bending-dominated; sheet gyroids sit in between and closer to stretch, which is why they beat the network form. Also a calibrated guess

lattice_strength_coefficient.description: C in sigma*/sigma_s = C rho^n for the lattice. Calibrated guess. Printed lattice strength is hit harder by surface roughness than stiffness is, because a rough as-built sheet is all notch

lattice_strength_exponent.description: n in sigma*/sigma_s = C rho^n. Calibrated guess
